Hi friends, happy Thursday!

The other day I was craving a big fat bowl of Honey Smacks cereal with whole milk. When I was a kid, that was luxury to me. But I hadn’t had them in forever so I didn’t even know if they were still around. 

You know me - I googled “HONEY SMACKS… DISCONTINUED??” Good news, they’re around. Bad news… I found out about Kellogg’s, the company that makes them, has been in some hot water lately. 

We all know inflation sucks and it’s affecting *everything*, especially food prices. Tons of families across America are struggling to put food on the table. 

So the media asked a Kelloggs CEO for his reaction on that. And his response? He essentially said, “MAYBE THEY SHOULD EAT CEREAL FOR DINNER.” 

Awkward. But this did get me thinking - why *do* we eat cereal for breakfast? Well I looked into it, and I stumbled into the world of John Harvey Kellogg, the man behind Kelloggs. And my mind was blown. 

Because behind that sweet little box of Honey Smacks is a freaky origin story. We’re talkin’ culty health retreats, yogurt enemas, and a crusade against masturbation. 

So buckle up if you dare, for the Dark History of …Kelloggs.

34:00 what you’re describing is a version of hardtack. 
If you were truly interested in this subject, you would look up hardtack. This is made from grain and some water and salt and maybe some oil it would be slowly baked and then it became a little hard. You’d add a bit more water and a little bit more oil and bake it again and bake it again and they just keep baking it maybe three times. and you would end up with HARD COMPRESSED biscuits of different sizes.
 Some probably the most common would be the size of a deck of cards or maybe twice that size. 
Now you would take this along with you when you traveled. Cowboys had it. They had it during the Civil War; during World War I. This was a way of having food with you that would not age that would not go bad. there are hard tech biscuits that survive that are hundreds of years old that if you wanted to you could eat today. However, you didn’t bite into it like you’re saying someone did and they broke their tooth. No you were supposed to break off a piece of it and soak it in water or it could be water with some honey in it, but usually if you’re out traveling or you live on the prairie or something, and you don’t have much, you might put a little salt in the water whatever you have. And it would soften it up and it would expand and then you could eat that. They also carried with them beef jerky. No refrigeration back then and if you’re a soldier what you have? Or if you’re a traveler, you don’t have any refrigeration or anything so in a cloth bag, you would keep your hardtack  biscuits and you would keep your beef jerky. And in your canteen, you would have water and there you are ! You could travel for days and you would know that you always have food. You don’t have to go hunting!
